study type: Prospective longitudinal cohort study with animal model experiments
exposure: Mode of birth (vaginal vs. cesarean delivery)
outcome: Gut microbiota composition (fecal microbiome, abundance of specific bacteria)
Mucosal immune system development (colonic lamina propria macrophage phenotypes, CX3CR1 protein, Il10 and Tgfb1 mRNAs, T-regulatory cell numbers)
cohort: The primary human cohort included 72 full-term and 49 preterm infants, with additional samples from 8 adults and 18 newborn infants (10 controls, 8 with necrotizing enterocolitis), complemented by studies in wild-type and S100a9-/- mice.
finding: S100A8 and S100A9 regulate the development of intestinal microbiota and the immune system in neonates, with low fecal levels associated with an altered microbiota composition and an increased risk of sepsis and obesity by age 2 years.
mod_finding: Infants born by cesarean delivery had lower fecal levels of S100A8-A9 compared to infants born by vaginal delivery.
